title: Amala
author: Testimony Adewale
desc: One cup of yam flour to two cups of water, with half a cup of hot water held back and poured into a well in the middle before it sits on low heat.
longDesc: Amala is the dark swallow of the Yoruba southwest, eaten under gbegiri and ewedu as abula. Elubo — yam flour — goes into water that is already bubbling, which is the opposite of how starch is made in the Delta, where everything starts cold. The detail that makes this recipe worth having is the reserved half cup: you hold water back, make a well in the centre of the mass, pour it in, and leave it alone. Lumps during the process are expected and are turned out at the end rather than prevented at the start.
ingredients: 1/2 cup hot water, held back for the well
steps: Heat the 2 cups of water until bubbling hot.
Remove some of the water and set it aside — this is the half cup you will pour back in later.
Reduce the heat and pour the yam flour in while stirring with the turning stick.
Keep stirring until the mixture comes together into a solid mass. Lumps at this stage are acceptable.
Make a circle in the centre of the mass and pour the reserved hot water into the middle.
Begin stirring and turning again until it is sticky and smooth.
Scoop onto a plate with a carving spoon, or wrap, and serve hot.
chefTips: The ratio is the thing: 1 cup of elubo to 2 cups of water. The Tribune prints it and a reader asking 9jafoodie for the ratio got the same answer back — 'one to two'.
The flour goes into hot water. That is the reverse of starch (NGA042), where the starch, water and oil all go into a cold pan together.
Hold the half cup back before the flour goes in, not after. Once the mass has formed you cannot measure it out.

The 35-minute simmer is long, and it is worth knowing that the same newspaper printed five minutes in a second article. Thirty-five gives a softer, more elastic amala; five gives you something you will have to work much harder with the stick.
Do not try to prevent lumps at the start. They go out in the final turning, which is what the long low simmer is buying you.
If you are not eating it straight away, wrap it while hot — amala skins over fast.
White yam flour and the darker elubo behave the same way here. The colour comes from how the yam was dried, not from the method.
commonMistakes: Pouring the flour into cold or warm water.
Adding all the water at once with no reserve.
Stirring through the simmer instead of leaving it covered and still.
Panicking at the lumps and adding more water.
Turning it out onto a cold plate and letting it skin.
sources: Quantities and method from 'Amala and Abula: Treat yourself to amazing Yoruba staple', byline Testimony Ishola, Tribune Online — 2 cups water, 1 cup yam flour, half a cup of hot water reserved, the well in the centre, the 35-minute low simmer, and the stated yield of 'one medium-sized serving'. This is the only named source consulted that publishes an amala ratio at all.

The 1:2 ratio is independently corroborated, but only in a comment: on 9jafoodie's 'Lump-free Amala' page — which carries no written recipe, no ingredient list and no method, only a video — a reader asked the elubo-to-water ratio and the site owner replied '1 to 2'.

DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled: a second Tribune Online article, 'Abula: Mix of Gbegiri and ewedu with Amala', byline 'Our Reporter', gives no quantities and specifies 'little warm water and leave to heat for five minutes' rather than thirty-five. Both figures are printed by the same newspaper. The 35 minutes is used here because it belongs to the article that actually quantifies the dish.

GAP: the isu / lafun / elubo / amala dudu taxonomy — white versus brown amala — is not addressed by any named source consulted. The Tribune article itself switches between 'yam flour' and 'yam/cassava flour' in consecutive steps without distinguishing them. Tola Akerele's 'Gbegiri and Ewedu with Amala' in The Orishirishi Cookbook (2020) is paywalled; only 'Serves: 6' is visible.

The named bloggers do not publish a written, quantified amala. Dooney's Kitchen's amala page returns 404 and All Nigerian Recipes' pounded yam and eba pages are video-only. The written record for the Yoruba swallows is thin because the instruction lives in video.
storage: Best eaten at once. It firms and dries within the hour.
reheating: Wrap in damp cling film and microwave in 30-second bursts, or steam briefly.
healthBenefits: Yam flour has a lower glycaemic response than cassava-based swallows.
Naturally fat-free as cooked — nothing is added but water.
A source of potassium and resistant starch.
culturalNote: Amala is Ibadan's calling card. The Tribune's second article on it puts the matter plainly: abula 'is common in Yorubaland, especially in Ibadan', and Tola Akerele's cookbook headnote says that if you want to impress someone from Ibadan, gbegiri and ewedu with amala is how. The buka — the roadside eating house — is where most people meet it.
